title: Environmental factors predicting blood lead levels in pregnant women in the UK: the ALSPAC study.
ehr_evidence: Whole blood samples were collected at median gestational age of 11 weeks and analysed by inductively coupled plasma dynamic reaction cell mass spectrometry (n = 4285). Self-completion postal questionnaires were used to collect data during pregnancy on lifestyle, diet and other environmental exposures.
summary: In a UK prospective cohort (ALSPAC) of 4285 pregnant women, environmental and lifestyle factors were modelled against blood lead levels measured by ICP-MS.
key_findings: Mean maternal BLL was 3.67 ± 1.47 mg/dl (geometric mean 3.43, median 3.42, range 0.41–19.14; n = 4285).
Highest educational qualification was the strongest independent predictor of BLL ≥5 mg/dl (odds ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.12–1.42; p <0.001).
Cigarette smoking, alcohol consumption, coffee consumption, and coal-fire home heating were independently associated with increased BLL (all p <0.001).
Dietary calcium intake (p = 0.001) and taking iron supplements (p = 0.046) were protective against high BLL.
The regression model explained 10.9% of the variance in BLL.
There was a significant correlation between maternal and child BLL (Pearson's r = 0.278, n = 233; p <0.001).
population: Pregnant women resident in the Avon area of the UK enrolled in ALSPAC (1991–1992), n = 4285
limitations: Sample bias: women with BLL measurement were older and had higher educational attainment than the rest of the ALSPAC cohort.
Environmental exposures (water, air, dust, occupation) were not included in the models, leaving ~89% of BLL variability unexplained.
Modest odds ratios for significant predictors.
Small sample sizes for some ethnic groups limited subgroup analyses.
